explanation: The urea cycle consumes 3 ATP molecules (equivalent to 4 high-energy phosphate bonds): 2 ATP for CPS I reaction and 1 ATP for argininosuccinate synthetase (AMP + PPi effectively = 2 ATP).
The main fate of urea is renal excretion in urine; approximately 20-25g of urea is filtered and excreted daily in adults, with small amounts lost in sweat.
N-acetylglutamate (NAG), synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate by N-acetylglutamate synthase, is the essential allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I.

The urea cycle and citric acid cycle are linked through fumarate (from argininosuccinate cleavage) which enters the TCA cycle, and aspartate (from TCA cycle transamination) which provides nitrogen for urea synthesis.
Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (or its cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin), preventing conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine.

PKU clinical features include intellectual disability (if untreated), hypopigmentation (decreased tyrosine reduces melanin), and characteristic mousy/musty odor from phenylacetate accumulation in urine and sweat.

PKU treatment involves lifelong dietary phenylalanine restriction with tyrosine supplementation (since tyrosine becomes essential); with defective BH4 metabolism, DOPA and 5-HTP supplementation is also required.
Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) results from deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, and valine and their ketoacids.

MSUD manifests as mental retardation, developmental delay, feeding difficulties, and characteristic sweet maple syrup/burnt sugar odor of urine from accumulating branched-chain ketoacids; untreated cases often fatal in infancy.
MSUD treatment requires lifelong restriction of branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine) in diet, with careful monitoring of amino acid levels to prevent neurological damage.

Morphine's effects are primarily mediated by mu (not kappa) opioid receptors; it also inhibits calcium influx (reducing transmitter release), increases K+ efflux (causing hyperpolarization), and reduces emotional pain response.
keyConcept: Mu vs kappa opioid receptor activation

explanation: Morphine is indicated for cancer pain, pulmonary edema (reduces preload and anxiety), and anesthesia adjunct; it is contraindicated in head injury (can worsen ICP and mask pupillary signs).
The most serious adverse effects of morphine are respiratory depression (potentially fatal) and psychological/physical dependence with tolerance development upon chronic use.
Morphine-induced constipation is relieved by stool softeners (docusate), stimulant laxatives, and peripherally-acting opioid antagonists (methylnaltrexone) that don't reverse analgesia.
Pethidine and tramadol both have analgesic properties and can cause seizures at high doses, but tramadol's action is only partially reversed by naloxone (has non-opioid mechanisms), unlike pethidine.
Neuropathic pain management includes tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline), anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, gabapentin), and atypical opioids (tramadol), all acting on different pain pathways.
The greater occipital nerve (C2 dorsal ramus) is the only scalp nerve derived from dorsal rami of spinal nerves; all other listed nerves are derived from ventral rami (cervical plexus).
keyConcept: Greater occipital nerve dorsal ramus origin

explanation: The posterior triangle is bounded by sternocleidomastoid, trapezius, and clavicle (not mandible); it is roofed by the superficial fascia and prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia.
The anterior triangle has four subdivisions (muscular, carotid, digastric, submental); the occipital triangle is part of the posterior triangle, not anterior triangle.

The tentorium cerebelli roofs over the posterior cranial fossa (not middle); its free border is attached to the anterior clinoid process (not post clinoid), and oculomotor/trochlear nerves pierce dura at this junction.
The falx cerebri separates the cerebral hemispheres and contains the superior sagittal sinus in its superior border; the diaphragma sellae separates the pituitary from the brain.
Denticulate ligaments are pial extensions that anchor the spinal cord to the dura mater laterally; the coccygeal ligament (filum terminale externum) attaches the cord terminus to the coccyx.
The ventral grey column contains dorsomedial, ventrolateral, intermediolateral, and central groups; the retrodorsolateral group is found in the dorsal horn (lamina IX), not ventral horn.
The hindbrain (rhombencephalon) includes medulla oblongata, pons, cerebellum, and fourth ventricle; the crus cerebri is part of the midbrain (mesencephalon), not hindbrain.
The brain stem includes midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata; the cerebellum and cerebral aqueduct are not part of the brain stem proper (cerebral aqueduct connects third and fourth ventricles).
The cranial part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) arises from the nucleus ambiguus in the medulla, carrying fibers that eventually join the vagus nerve to innervate laryngeal muscles.

The right spinal lemniscus carries pain and temperature sensation from the left side of the body (crossed fibers from spinothalamic tract); proprioception is carried in the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway.
The gracile and cuneate tracts are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries (branches of vertebral artery) and radicular arteries; the anterior spinal artery supplies anterior cord structures.

In adults, lumbar puncture is performed at L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace (below L2 where spinal cord terminates); the needle passes through skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura, and arachnoid.
